verdict.root_cause: No root cause was established. Six of seven dispatches returned tool failures or non-existent series rather than observations: both change-history queries died on a payload parse error at the 10,000-character boundary [tr_99e786adb0bd, tr_743335484daa], both log queries were rejected by Loki with HTTP 400 due to an invalid escaped-hyphen pod regex that was never corrected [tr_3644135888c3, tr_4f0bef88fe0e], and the span-metric error ratios for product-catalog and frontend were empty in incident and baseline windows alike, meaning the series does not exist rather than having dropped at onset [tr_bad85b91580f, tr_e35679d06e1f]. The only substantive signal is the trace sample [tr_d40c56f3c0c4], and it points away from product-catalog: its server spans finish in 0.8-9.3ms with sub-2ms postgresql children and no error status, and the frontend->product-catalog hop is clean on both sides. The 0.8-2.2s user-facing latency sits almost entirely in load-generator client GET self time, with the whole frontend+product-catalog subtree occupying ~3-21ms at the tail of each trace - an un-instrumented wait on the load-generator->frontend edge. On this evidence the failing mechanism cannot be named.
verdict.reasoning: The trace sample actively excludes the obvious candidates: no callee-propagated database failure (postgresql children all under 2ms, unmarked), no failing frontend->product-catalog hop (every client span has a matching completed server child), and product-catalog's subtree is milliseconds at the end of multi-second traces [tr_d40c56f3c0c4]. What remains is a seconds-long wait accruing in the caller before the frontend server span starts, so the frontend is the service named - but whether it is slow to accept connections, briefly unreachable, or whether the load generator itself is the stall cannot be separated. The channels that would separate them all failed: product-catalog logs were never read [tr_3644135888c3, tr_4f0bef88fe0e], change history was never read and the second query's window started at onset and ran forward [tr_743335484daa], and the metric channel can support neither a spike nor health [tr_bad85b91580f, tr_e35679d06e1f]. Naming bad_config, bad_deploy or feature_flag would mean inventing a mechanism from a change log nobody successfully read.
open_questions: What product-catalog and frontend logged at onset - the Loki query must be reissued with a valid matcher (pod=~"product-catalog-.*") before silence, exceptions, or flag text can be claimed.
What changed before 02:26:33 - both change queries failed, and one used a window starting at onset running forward, so it could not have answered even on success; re-run backward with pagination.

Where the load-generator client GET self time is actually spent: connection setup, frontend accept backlog, or load-generator-side scheduling - no frontend-side logs, resource metrics, or ingress data were gathered.

alternatives.root_cause: frontend is saturated (threads, connections, or CPU) and callers queue before their requests are accepted, producing caller-side self time with fast downstream spans.
alternatives.why_not: Fits the trace shape, but no frontend resource metric, log line, or pod state was ever collected; the only frontend dispatch returned a non-existent metric series [tr_e35679d06e1f].

alternatives.root_cause: The load generator itself is the bottleneck (client-side contention or deliberate pacing), and no production service is faulty.
alternatives.why_not: Would explain 100%-self-time client spans and the lone orphan ERROR POST span, but load-generator was never dispatched against, and a critical multi-service alert is unlikely to be purely synthetic.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no effect is predicted. The correct next step is investigative, not remedial: reissue the Loki query with a valid matcher (pod=~"product-catalog-.*") and re-run change_history backward from 02:26:33 with pagination or a shorter window, then gather frontend-side resource/ingress data to locate the 0.8-2.2s load-generator client GET self time. None of those are actions this system may take.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention would be shown wrong if the reissued change-history query returns a deploy, image, or flag change on product-catalog or frontend inside the incident window - that would meet rollback_image or revert_config preconditions and make a targeted proposal defensible. It would also be shown wrong if corrected logs reveal a crash-loop or wedged-process signature on frontend, which would meet restart_service's precondition. Until one of those lands, any action here is a guess.
proposal.risk: Acting now is the risk being avoided. The only substantive evidence [tr_d40c56f3c0c4] points away from product-catalog: its server spans complete in 0.8-9.3ms with sub-2ms postgresql children and no error status, and the frontend->product-catalog hop is clean on both sides. Rolling back or restarting product-catalog or frontend on this basis would destroy in-process cache, reset live connections, and likely leave the 0.8-2.2s latency untouched while consuming the incident window and corrupting the evidence trail - and a rollback has no recorded prior image tag to return to, since both change queries failed.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal, as nothing is changed. For context on what was declined: a product-catalog action would be seen by frontend, checkout and recommendation as inbound callers; a frontend action would be seen by frontend-proxy and load-generator. Those callers remain untouched.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical severity with product-catalog alerting alongside the load generator and a multi-hop blast radius touching checkout and frontend — not dismissible as a single warning-latency case. No open incidents to attribute it to, and nothing in the signal yet favors a specific fault class.
